story.title: All Rescued After Tanker Collision with Cruise Ship on Mississippi River
story.summary: A tanker collided with a luxury paddle wheeler docked in New Orleans, causing the cruise vessel to roll over and sink. Fortunately, all passengers were rescued without fatalities, leading to the incident being referred to as a 'miracle on the Mississippi.' In response, New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit seeking at least $1 million in damages and requesting control of the tanker involved in the crash.

event_overview.title: About Mississippi River Incident
event_overview.subject: Mississippi River Incident
event_overview.summary: The Mississippi River Incident is the November 13, 2026 marine casualty in which the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck American Cruise Lines’ docked paddlewheeler American Heritage at the Port of New Orleans. The passenger vessel took on water and capsized, prompting a multiagency rescue; American Cruise Lines said all passengers and crew were safely accounted for, while the cause remained under investigation.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The allision occurred around 12:30 p.m. local time on November 13, 2026, on the Mississippi River beside the Port of New Orleans administration building; the American Heritage had been docked and was beginning passenger disembarkation.

facts.label: Vessels involved
facts.value: The moving vessel was the tanker Atlantic Asphalt; the stationary passenger vessel was American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage, a Mississippi River paddlewheeler.

facts.label: Passenger vessel profile
facts.value: American Cruise Lines lists the American Heritage as a 2015-built paddlewheeler with a 150-guest capacity, operating on the Mississippi River.

facts.label: Rescue outcome
facts.value: American Cruise Lines reported on November 14 that all passengers and crew had been evacuated and were safe and accounted for.

facts.label: Investigation
facts.value: The National Transportation Safety Board deployed investigators; as of November 14, its expected timetable was a preliminary report within about 30 days and a final report, including probable cause findings, in roughly 18 to 24 months.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the initial November 14-15 rescue and accounting developments, not the full salvage operation, litigation, or the eventual official findings on cause and responsibility.

explore_lenses.label: What does taking control of the tanker change?
explore_lenses.title: The port is securing a potential source of payment
explore_lenses.summary: The Port of New Orleans is using a federal maritime case to preserve its ability to recover claimed terminal and response costs; the seizure process is not a finding that the tanker operator is legally at fault.

claims.text: The port's suit names the tanker Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and manager Thome Ship Management, and alleges terminal damage exceeding $1 million plus further cleanup, inspection, repair and salvage expenses.
A federal judge issued a warrant placing the tanker under federal control for now, after the port sought its arrest and possible sale to satisfy its maritime claim.
Thome said the tanker was stably anchored after separation from the riverboat and that it was cooperating with authorities; this is the manager's account, not an investigative conclusion.

explore_lenses.label: Why is the cause still unknown?
explore_lenses.title: Investigators have key evidence, but no conclusion
explore_lenses.summary: The NTSB has opened an ongoing marine investigation and recovered the tanker’s voyage data recorder, which can help reconstruct movement and bridge activity. Early reports of a steering problem are not a confirmed cause.

claims.text: The NTSB records that the Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked American Heritage at about 1:02 p.m. CST on November 13, 2026, at mile 96 on the Lower Mississippi River.
The NTSB investigation is ongoing; its public page does not yet list findings, a probable cause or safety recommendations.
NTSB investigators recovered the tanker’s voyage data recorder and planned witness interviews; the recorder includes operational data such as speed, course and bridge audio.
Forecast: NTSB member John DeLeeuw said a preliminary report is expected within about 30 days and a final report in roughly 18 to 24 months.

explore_lenses.label: What must happen before recovery is complete?
explore_lenses.title: Salvage and pollution prevention are immediate priorities
explore_lenses.summary: Even with all people accounted for, the capsized vessel and damaged terminal leave a complex recovery operation. Officials are balancing safe salvage, fuel removal and restoration of river traffic.

claims.text: The American Heritage remains on its side at the terminal, while the Atlantic Asphalt has been towed away from the immediate scene.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said response work was focused on reopening the river and safely removing hazardous material from the American Heritage; officials were monitoring for pollution and restricting nearby vessel traffic.
Forecast: Burnham said removing the riverboat could take weeks, pending diver assessments and a salvage approach.

story_report.summary: A tanker collided with the docked luxury paddle wheeler American Heritage in New Orleans, leaving the cruise vessel on its side and sunk after the impact. All passengers were rescued, with no fatalities reported in the evidence packet. The crash has disrupted operations at the terminal, prompted a federal investigation and led the Port of New Orleans to pursue more than $1 million in claimed damages while seeking control of the tanker through maritime court proceedings.

sections.heading: NTSB Investigation Into River Collision
sections.body: The National Transportation Safety Board says the Atlantic Asphalt struck the docked American Heritage at about 1:02 p.m. CST on Nov. 13, 2026, near mile 96 on the Lower Mississippi River. Investigators recovered the tanker's voyage data recorder, which contains information including speed, course and bridge audio, and planned witness interviews. The agency has not yet published findings, a probable cause or safety recommendations.

sections.heading: Port Seeks Tanker Arrest and Damages
sections.body: The port's lawsuit names the Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and manager Thome Ship Management. It alleges terminal damage exceeding $1 million and seeks additional cleanup, inspection, repair and salvage costs. A federal judge issued a warrant placing the tanker under federal control for now after the port sought its arrest and a possible sale to satisfy its maritime claim. Thome has said the tanker was stably anchored after separating from the riverboat and that it is cooperating with authorities.

sections.heading: Salvage Operations and River Restrictions
sections.body: The American Heritage remains on its side at the terminal, while the Atlantic Asphalt has been towed from the immediate area. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said responders were working to reopen the river and safely remove hazardous material from the riverboat, while monitoring for pollution and restricting nearby vessel traffic. Burnham said removal of the riverboat could take weeks, pending diver assessments and a salvage plan.

unresolved.text: Investigators have not determined whether steering, propulsion, navigation, crew actions, river conditions or another factor caused the collision. An NTSB preliminary report is expected in about 30 days, with a final report projected in roughly 18 to 24 months.
The court has not determined fault, the final recoverable damages or whether additional parties will be added to the case.
Officials have not announced a final salvage timetable, terminal-repair plan or final environmental-impact assessment.

Trump has criticized the decision and indicated plans to appeal the ruling.
